title: Level 2 Chemistry: Bonding, Structure, Properties and Energy Changes -- 2024
subject: chemistry

questions.text:
Draw the Lewis structure for each of the two blank molecules, and name their shapes.

A table is given with three molecules: NCl3 (nitrogen trichloride), H2O (water), and CO2 (carbon dioxide).

H2O is provided as an example: Lewis structure H-O-H, shape 'bent', bond angle 104.5 degrees.

NCl3 has bond angle 107 degrees. CO2 has bond angle 180 degrees.

Draw the Lewis structures for NCl3 and CO2, and name their shapes.
questions.expectedAnswer: NCl3: Lewis structure shows N with three Cl atoms bonded and one lone pair on N. Shape: trigonal pyramidal. CO2: Lewis structure shows O=C=O with two double bonds and no lone pairs on C. Shape: linear.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Draws a correct Lewis structure OR identifies the correct shape and bond angles. Merit: Links lone pairs and bonding regions to geometry. Excellence: Explains bond angles and shapes by referring to electron repulsion including lone pairs.

questions.text:
Compare and contrast the shapes and bond angles of aluminium trichloride, AlCl3, and phosphorus trichloride, PCl3.

AlCl3: Al central atom with 3 Cl atoms and no lone pairs on the central atom (trigonal planar).
PCl3: P central atom with 3 Cl atoms and one lone pair on P.

Compare and contrast the shapes and bond angles of these molecules.
questions.expectedAnswer: AlCl3 is trigonal planar with bond angles of 120 degrees, as the Al central atom has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the three regions of electron density repel equally. PCl3 is trigonal pyramidal with bond angles of approximately 107 degrees; the lone pair on phosphorus repels the bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the Cl-P-Cl bond angles below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5 degrees.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies the correct shape of ONE molecule. Merit: Links lone pairs to shape for ONE molecule. Excellence: Explains both shapes with reference to electron repulsion.

questions.text:
Water, H2O, and carbon dioxide, CO2, have different shapes, but they have different polarities.

Circle the word below which identifies the polarity of H2O.

Polar          Non-polar

Justify your choice of polarity by:
- explaining the links between the bonding and structure of each substance, and
- relating this to how the polarity of a molecule is determined.
questions.expectedAnswer: H2O is polar because the O-H bonds are polar (electronegativity difference) and the bent shape means the dipoles do not cancel. CO2 is non-polar because although C=O bonds are polar, the linear symmetrical arrangement means the dipoles cancel.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies polarity OR electronegativity difference. Merit: Links asymmetry to non-cancellation for one molecule. Excellence: Justifies polarity of BOTH molecules.

questions.text:
Ethanamine, CH3CH2NH2, is used in the production of herbicides and pharmaceuticals.

Although hydrogen cyanide, HCN, is highly poisonous, it can be used to produce ethanamine, as shown:

2HCN(g) + 5H2(g) -> CH3CH2NH2(g) + NH3(g)    DH = -318 kJ mol-1

Calculate the mass of ethanamine formed when 2650 kJ of energy is released.
M(CH3CH2NH2) = 45.1 g mol-1
questions.expectedAnswer:
n(CH3CH2NH2) = 2650 / 318 = 8.333 mol (1 mol of ethanamine is formed per 318 kJ released)
m = n x M = 8.333 x 45.1 = 375.8 g (376 g, 3 s.f.)
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: One step correct. Merit: Correct answer for one part. Excellence: Correct answer with units.

questions.text:
Choose the correct energy diagram that represents the reaction above and label it with the information provided in the equation.

Two energy diagrams are shown: the left diagram shows reactants at a high energy level dropping to a lower products level. The right diagram shows reactants at a low level rising to a higher products level.
questions.expectedAnswer: The LEFT diagram is correct (exothermic, DH is negative).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies correct energy diagram. Merit: Correct diagram with labels.

questions.text:
The table below shows four substances in their solid states.

Complete the table by filling in the missing information for each substance.
questions.expectedAnswer: SiO2: covalent network, atoms, strong covalent bonds. SCl2: molecular, molecules, weak intermolecular forces. NaCl: ionic, ions, strong ionic bonds. Ag: metallic, metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons, metallic bonds.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Two rows correct. Merit: Full table correct.

questions.text:
Both SiO2 and SCl2 contain similar elements, but SCl2 has a considerably lower melting point.

Explain why there is a difference in melting point for these substances.
questions.expectedAnswer: SiO2 is a 3D covalent network solid held together by strong covalent bonds requiring large amounts of energy to break. SCl2 is a molecular solid held together by weak intermolecular forces requiring little energy to overcome.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies melting point is linked to force strength. Merit: Links forces to energy for ONE substance. Excellence: Compares both substances.

questions.text:
Explain why sulfur dichloride, SCl2, does not dissolve in water, but sodium chloride, NaCl, does.

In your answer:
- link to their structure and bonding
- include the type of solvent that SCl2 will dissolve in, and why
- include a diagram to support your answer for NaCl.
questions.expectedAnswer: SCl2 is a polar molecular substance but has only weak dipole-dipole and dispersion forces; although SCl2 is slightly polar it does not form hydrogen bonds, so it does not dissolve well in water and instead dissolves better in non-polar or low-polarity solvents (like dissolves like). NaCl is ionic; the polar water molecules surround the Na+ and Cl- ions (the partially negative O ends of water attract Na+, and the partially positive H ends attract Cl-), overcoming the ionic bonds and dissolving the solid.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies SCl2 as non-polar OR identifies attractions needed. Merit: Links forces to solubility for ONE solute. Excellence: Full explanation for both.

questions.text:
Bottled gas (LPG) supply in New Zealand is a mix of ethane, C2H6, and propane, C3H8.

Energy released by ethane combustion:
2C2H6(g) + 7O2(g) -> 4CO2(g) + 6H2O(g)    DH = -3122 kJ mol-1 (i.e. -1561 kJ per mole of C2H6)
M(C2H6) = 30.1 g mol-1

Calculate the energy released by 1.50 kg of ethane.
questions.expectedAnswer:
n(ethane) = 1500 / 30.1 = 49.83 mol
Energy = 49.83 x 1561 = 77,800 kJ released (3 s.f.)
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: One step correct. Merit: Correct answer.

questions.text:
Energy released by propane combustion:
C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) -> 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(g)    DH = -2220 kJ mol-1
M(C3H8) = 44.1 g mol-1

Calculate the energy released by 1.50 kg of propane.
questions.expectedAnswer:
n(propane) = 1500 / 44.1 = 34.01 mol
Energy = 34.01 x 2220 = 75,500 kJ released (3 s.f.)
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: One step correct. Merit: Correct answer.

questions.text: Calculate how much more energy is released by 1.50 kg of ethane than 1.50 kg of propane.
questions.expectedAnswer: Difference = 77,800 - 75,500 = 2,300 kJ. Ethane releases about 2,300 kJ more energy per 1.50 kg compared to propane.

questions.text:
The reaction of a methane fuel cell is shown below. Methane reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.

CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(g)    DH = -802 kJ mol-1

Bond energies: C-H = 413 kJ mol-1, O=O = 498 kJ mol-1, C=O = 805 kJ mol-1

Use the bond energies listed and the change in enthalpy (-802 kJ mol-1) to calculate the average bond energy of the O-H bond.
questions.expectedAnswer:
Bonds broken: 4 x C-H = 4 x 413 = 1652 kJ; 2 x O=O = 2 x 498 = 996 kJ. Total broken = 2648 kJ.
Bonds formed in products: 2 x C=O (in CO2) = 2 x 805 = 1610 kJ; 4 x O-H (in 2 H2O) = 4x.
DH = bonds broken - bonds formed: -802 = 2648 - (1610 + 4x). Rearranging: 4x = 2648 + 802 - 1610 = 1840. x = 460 kJ mol-1. Average O-H bond energy = 460 kJ mol-1.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correctly calculates total bonds broken OR formed. Merit: Correct process with minor error. Excellence: Correct answer with units.

questions.text:
Fullerene is an allotrope of carbon that is strong, lightweight, and has excellent conductivity. Like graphite, fullerene conducts electricity.

What requirement must fullerene have to allow it to conduct electricity?
questions.expectedAnswer: To conduct electricity, a substance must contain free-moving charged particles (delocalised electrons).

questions.text:
Aluminium, Al, is also a good conductor of electricity, and it is malleable (can be pressed into shapes). These properties enable it to be used extensively in wiring and for components in electronics.

Explain why copper, Cu, has these properties, and link it to the uses stated.

Refer to its structure and bonding.
questions.expectedAnswer: Cu is a metallic solid with metal cations in a 3D lattice surrounded by delocalised valence electrons. The delocalised electrons can move freely, carrying charge (conductivity). The non-directional metallic bonds allow layers to slide without breaking (malleability).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describes metallic structure. Merit: Links conductivity to delocalised electrons OR malleability to non-directional bonds. Excellence: Explains both properties and links to uses.
